subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
Why sperm are small and many, eggs large and few
What happens at fertilization in humans
Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
Self-incompatibility keeps gametes from different plants
Making sperm and making eggs
From zygote to blastocyst to implantation
Progesterone keeps pregnancy going; its fall lets birth begin
Haploid gametes fuse to make a diploid zygote
Phenotype: genotype plus environment
PKU: a recessive condition
ABO blood groups: three alleles
Haemophilia is X-linked
Box-and-whisker plots
Dihybrid ratios: 9:3:3:1 and 1:1:1:1
Spotting recombinants in a test cross
What homeostasis keeps steady
Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
The loop of Henle salts the medulla

questions.q: What is the relative advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
options: Its offspring carry new gene combinations, giving the variation needed for a changed environment.
Its offspring gain the particular features that a changed environment comes to require.
Its offspring are better adapted than the parent in every environment, so more of them survive.
Its offspring carry new alleles produced by meiosis, which asexual offspring cannot receive.
optionWhy: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with new combinations of alleles, so among them some are likely to be adapted to an environment that has changed. This is its relative advantage; asexual reproduction's is the faithful copying of a genotype already adapted to the existing environment.
A student who thinks variation is produced to meet a need picks this. Meiosis and fertilization generate new combinations blindly; the environment selects among them afterwards.
A student who believes sexual reproduction is always superior picks this. In a stable environment a well-adapted parent does better to copy its genotype asexually than to break it up.
A student who thinks meiosis makes new alleles picks this. New alleles arise only by mutation, in asexual lineages too; meiosis and fertilization produce new combinations of existing alleles.
questions.explain: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with new combinations of alleles, so among them some are likely to be adapted to an environment that has changed. This is its relative advantage; asexual reproduction's is the faithful copying of a genotype already adapted to the existing environment.

questions.q: In a fish species the female lays a few hundred large eggs in a nest and the male releases many millions of tiny sperm over them. Which statement explains the difference in size and number?
options: Sperm must travel to the eggs, so they are small with few food reserves and can be produced cheaply in vast numbers.
Eggs are larger because each one carries far more of the genetic material than a sperm does.
The numbers should be equal since one sperm fertilizes one egg; the surplus sperm are defective ones.
Sperm are small because so many are made that only a little cytoplasm is available for each one.
optionWhy: The prime difference between the sexes is that the male gamete travels to the female gamete, so it is smaller with less food reserves than the egg. From this follow the differences in numbers of gametes.
A student who equates cell size with DNA content picks this. Sperm and egg each contribute one haploid set; the egg's extra bulk is cytoplasm with food reserves.
A student who reasons back from one-to-one fertilization picks this. Vast numbers of normal sperm are released because only a tiny fraction complete the journey to an egg.
A student who reverses the cause picks this. Sperm are small because they must travel; being small and cheap is what makes it possible to produce so many.
questions.explain: The prime difference between the sexes is that the male gamete travels to the female gamete, so it is smaller with less food reserves than the egg. From this follow the differences in numbers of gametes.

questions.q: Which event occurs during fertilization in humans?
options: The whole sperm enters the egg, so the embryo inherits its mitochondria from both parents.
The sperm and egg nuclei fuse into a single diploid nucleus before any cell division occurs.
The sperm nucleus enters the egg but the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed.
Enzymes from the sperm digest a hole in the egg membrane to let the nucleus in.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the sperm entering as a complete cell picks this. Only the nucleus enters; the tail and mitochondria are destroyed.
A student who learned 'the nuclei fuse' at GCSE picks this. The nuclear membranes dissolve and the chromosomes join a mitosis that directly produces two diploid nuclei.
After the sperm's cell membrane fuses with the egg cell membrane, the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the tail and mitochondria do not contribute to the zygote.
A student who extends the acrosome enzymes to the egg membrane picks this. Entry is by fusion of the two cell membranes; enzymes act only on the coat outside the membrane.
questions.explain: After the sperm's cell membrane fuses with the egg cell membrane, the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the tail and mitochondria do not contribute to the zygote.

questions.q: Where are the gametes of a flowering plant produced?
options: The pollen grains themselves are the male gametes and the ovules are the female gametes.
Male gametes are produced inside pollen grains and female gametes inside ovules.
Male gametes are produced in the stigma and female gametes in the anther.
Male gametes are produced inside pollen grains and female gametes in the seeds.
optionWhy: A student who casts pollen as the plant's sperm picks this. Pollen grains and ovules are structures inside which the gametes are produced.
Gametes are produced inside ovules (female, within the ovary) and inside pollen grains (male, within the anther); pollination and pollen tube growth bring them together.
A student who has swapped the two central structures picks this. The anther produces pollen (male); the stigma receives it and belongs to the female carpel.
A student who backdates seeds to the flower picks this. The ovary contains ovules; an ovule becomes a seed only after its gamete has been fertilized.
questions.explain: Gametes are produced inside ovules (female, within the ovary) and inside pollen grains (male, within the anther); pollination and pollen tube growth bring them together.

questions.q: In a self-incompatible plant species, pollen from a flower lands on the stigma of the same flower and germinates, but no seed is set. Which statement about self-incompatibility explains this?
options: It works by physically preventing the flower's own pollen from ever landing on its stigma.
It prevents inbreeding, which would otherwise cause harmful new mutations in the offspring.
It stops a plant's own pollen from fertilizing its eggs, so preventing inbreeding.
It is needed because self-fertilization would be asexual and so produce clones.
optionWhy: A student who models it on separate flowers and timing picks this. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism: matching alleles in pollen and carpel are recognized and the pollen tube is stopped.
A student who explains genetic defects by mutation picks this. Inbreeding makes harmful recessive alleles already present more likely to be homozygous; it creates no alleles.
Self-pollination leads to inbreeding, which decreases genetic diversity and vigour. Genetic self-incompatibility mechanisms ensure the gametes fusing at fertilization are from different plants.
A student who thinks one parent means asexual picks this. Self-fertilization is still sexual reproduction; the problem is inbreeding, not cloning.
questions.explain: Self-pollination leads to inbreeding, which decreases genetic diversity and vigour. Genetic self-incompatibility mechanisms ensure the gametes fusing at fertilization are from different plants.

questions.q: Which comparison of spermatogenesis and oogenesis in humans is correct?
options: Each meiosis yields four gametes in both processes, but three of every four eggs degenerate before birth.
Both processes continue to produce new gametes from puberty right through to old age.
Each meiosis yields four sperm but only one egg, because oogenesis divides the cytoplasm unequally.
In both processes the two divisions of meiosis are completed inside the gonad before the gamete is released.
optionWhy: A student who applies the 'four cells from meiosis' rule to eggs picks this. In oogenesis the cytoplasm divides unequally, so each meiosis gives one egg and small polar bodies.
A student who generalizes from sperm picks this. All egg-forming cells are made before birth; only spermatogenesis continues producing new gametes throughout adult life.

In spermatogenesis the two divisions of meiosis give four equal cells that differentiate into sperm; in oogenesis each division is unequal, producing one large egg with most of the cytoplasm and polar bodies that degenerate.
A student who assumes the ovulated cell is a finished gamete picks this. The second meiotic division of oogenesis is completed only after a sperm enters the egg.
questions.explain: In spermatogenesis the two divisions of meiosis give four equal cells that differentiate into sperm; in oogenesis each division is unequal, producing one large egg with most of the cytoplasm and polar bodies that degenerate.

questions.q: Which statement about the blastocyst and implantation is correct?
options: The zygote itself implants in the endometrium immediately after fertilization, before it has divided into a ball of cells.
The blastocyst is a hollow ball with an inner cell mass and implants in the endometrium about a week after fertilization.
The blastocyst is a solid ball of identical cells, every one of which goes on to form part of the foetus.
The blastocyst forms and implants in the uterus, at the same site where fertilization took place.
optionWhy: A student who runs fertilization straight into implantation picks this. The zygote divides for several days on its way to the uterus, and only the blastocyst implants.
By about day 5 to 7 the embryo is a blastocyst: a hollow ball with a fluid-filled cavity, an inner cell mass that forms the foetus and an outer layer that attaches to and sinks into the endometrium.
A student who thinks all the early cells are equivalent picks this. The blastocyst is hollow and its outer layer contributes to the placenta, not the foetus.
A student who places fertilization in the uterus picks this. Fertilization occurs in the oviduct; the blastocyst forms during transit and implants in the endometrium.
questions.explain: By about day 5 to 7 the embryo is a blastocyst: a hollow ball with a fluid-filled cavity, an inner cell mass that forms the foetus and an outer layer that attaches to and sinks into the endometrium.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the hormonal changes that bring about childbirth?
options: Progesterone falls, contractions begin, and oxytocin rises by positive feedback as the cervix is stretched.
Progesterone rises to a peak that triggers contractions, and oxytocin then falls until the baby is born.
Oxytocin is kept at a steady level by negative feedback so that the contractions stay regular.
The pituitary gland stops secreting progesterone, allowing it to secrete oxytocin in its place.
optionWhy: A decrease in progesterone removes the inhibition of uterine contractions and allows oxytocin secretion to increase; stretching of the cervix stimulates more oxytocin release, a positive feedback loop that continues until birth.
A student who expects a rising hormone to trigger the event picks this. Progesterone keeps the uterus relaxed; it is its fall that allows childbirth to start.
A student who assumes all hormonal control is negative feedback picks this. Oxytocin secretion rises progressively by positive feedback during labour.
A student who places progesterone in the pituitary picks this. Progesterone comes from the corpus luteum and then the placenta; the pituitary secretes oxytocin.
questions.explain: A decrease in progesterone removes the inhibition of uterine contractions and allows oxytocin secretion to increase; stretching of the cervix stimulates more oxytocin release, a positive feedback loop that continues until birth.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the means of inheritance in eukaryotes that have a sexual life cycle?
options: Each parent produces haploid gametes by meiosis, and their fusion forms a diploid zygote with two copies of each autosomal gene
Each parent's gametes carry both of its alleles of every gene, so the zygote's traits blend the two parental genotypes
Haploid gametes fusing to form a zygote is the pattern in animals, while plants pass on their genes through pollen and seeds instead
Each gamete carries the parent's single copy of each gene, so the zygote formed at fertilization has one copy of each gene
optionWhy: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that each gamete carries one copy of each autosomal gene; fertilization restores the diploid number, giving the zygote two copies, one from each parent. This pattern is common to all sexually reproducing eukaryotes.

A student who thinks a parent passes on its whole genotype picks this. Gametes are haploid and carry only one allele of each gene, chosen at random in meiosis, and the alleles remain separate in the zygote rather than blending.

A student who files plant reproduction as a separate process picks this. Pollen contains male gametes and the ovule contains the female gamete; their fusion forms a diploid zygote, so plants follow the same haploid–diploid pattern as animals.

A student who pictures a gene as a single object in the cell picks this. A diploid parent has two copies of each autosomal gene and puts one into each gamete; the zygote therefore has two copies, one on each homologous chromosome.
questions.explain: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that each gamete carries one copy of each autosomal gene; fertilization restores the diploid number, giving the zygote two copies, one from each parent. This pattern is common to all sexually reproducing eukaryotes.

questions.q: Which list gives a human trait due to genotype only, then a trait due to environment only, then a trait due to interaction between genotype and environment, in that order?
options: Adult height; a facial scar; skin colour
ABO blood group; adult height; a facial scar
ABO blood group; skin colour; adult height
ABO blood group; a scar; adult height
optionWhy: A student who thinks inherited traits are fixed by the genes alone files height as genotype only. Height is strongly influenced by nutrition and health during growth, so it is an interaction trait, not a genotype-only one.

A student who treats any observable trait as part of the heritable phenotype puts the scar with the traits that involve genotype. A scar is due to the environment only, and height, listed here as environment only, has a clear genetic component.

A student who credits sunlight with all variation in skin colour puts it as environment only. Skin colour depends on several genes as well as on exposure to sunlight, so it is an interaction trait, like height.

ABO blood group is set entirely by the alleles inherited; a scar has no genetic basis; adult height depends on the alleles inherited and on environmental factors such as nutrition during growth, so it results from interaction between genotype and environment.
questions.explain: ABO blood group is set entirely by the alleles inherited; a scar has no genetic basis; adult height depends on the alleles inherited and on environmental factors such as nutrition during growth, so it results from interaction between genotype and environment.

questions.q: PKU usually appears in a child whose parents are both unaffected. Which statement correctly describes phenylketonuria (PKU)?
options: It is caused by a dominant allele of an autosomal gene, which is why the condition is expressed in every person who carries it
It is caused by a recessive allele that prevents the body making phenylalanine, so affected people need extra phenylalanine in their diet
It is caused by a recessive allele of an autosomal gene coding for the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine
It is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome, so it is expressed in males far more often than in females
optionWhy: A student who reasons that a condition that is expressed must be dominant picks this. PKU appears only in people homozygous for the mutant allele; heterozygous carriers are unaffected, which is the signature of a recessive allele.

A student who takes the name to mean a shortage of phenylalanine picks this. The missing enzyme converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, so phenylalanine accumulates and the treatment is a diet low in phenylalanine, not rich in it.

PKU is a recessive genetic condition due to mutation in an autosomal gene for the enzyme needed to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. A homozygous recessive person lacks the functional enzyme, so phenylalanine accumulates.

A student who assumes that any recessive disorder appearing in the children of unaffected parents is sex-linked picks this. The PKU gene is autosomal, so the condition is equally frequent in males and females.
questions.explain: PKU is a recessive genetic condition due to mutation in an autosomal gene for the enzyme needed to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. A homozygous recessive person lacks the functional enzyme, so phenylalanine accumulates.

questions.q: A woman with blood group A whose genotype is IAi has children with a man of blood group B whose genotype is IBi. Which blood groups are possible in their children, and with what probabilities?
options: Groups A, B and AB, each 1 in 3, but not group O, as neither parent is group O
Groups AB, A, B and O are all possible, each with a probability of 1 in 4
Groups A and AB only, each 1 in 2, because the IA allele is dominant to IB
Groups A and B only, each 1 in 2, since each parent passes on its own group's allele
optionWhy: A student who thinks a child's blood group must match a parent's picks this. Both parents carry the recessive allele i, and an ii child, group O, is produced in 1 in 4 fertilizations.

The Punnett grid for IAi × IBi gives IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), one cell each. IA and IB are codominant and both dominant to i, so all four ABO groups are possible with equal probability.
A student who forces the three alleles into a dominant/recessive hierarchy picks this. IA and IB are codominant, so IAIB is group AB, and IBi is group B; the option also ignores the ii children.

A student who treats blood group as a unit trait that a child takes from one parent or the other picks this. Each parent is heterozygous and passes on either of its two alleles with equal probability, so four genotypes, IAIB, IAi, IBi and ii, are possible, giving all four blood groups.
questions.explain: The Punnett grid for IAi × IBi gives IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), one cell each. IA and IB are codominant and both dominant to i, so all four ABO groups are possible with equal probability.

questions.q: Why is haemophilia far more common in males than in females?
options: The allele is carried on the Y chromosome, so that a father passes the condition directly to each one of his sons
Females who inherit the allele can only ever be carriers, because the female body cannot develop the condition
Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele produces the condition, whereas a female needs two
The Y chromosome carries a second copy of the gene that is more often mutated than the copy on the X
optionWhy: A student who expects a male-biased condition to pass from father to son picks this. The gene is on the X chromosome; a father gives his Y to sons, so sons inherit the haemophilia allele only from their mother.

A student who believes females cannot have haemophilia picks this. A female with two Xh alleles does have haemophilia; the condition is rare in females because inheriting Xh from both parents is much less likely.

The haemophilia allele is recessive and on the X chromosome. A male XhY has no second X to carry a dominant allele, so he has haemophilia; a female must be XhXh, which requires an affected father and a carrier or affected mother and is therefore rare.

A student who thinks the X and Y carry the same genes picks this. The Y chromosome carries far fewer genes than the X and has no copy of the haemophilia gene, which is precisely why males have only one copy.
questions.explain: The haemophilia allele is recessive and on the X chromosome. A male XhY has no second X to carry a dominant allele, so he has haemophilia; a female must be XhXh, which requires an affected father and a carrier or affected mother and is therefore rare.

questions.q: For a class's heights, the first quartile is 150 cm, the median is 158 cm, the third quartile is 166 cm, and the minimum and maximum are 130 cm and 192 cm. Above what height would a data point be categorized as an outlier on a box-and-whisker plot?
options: 190 cm
182 cm
174 cm
259 cm
optionWhy: The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1 = 166 − 150 = 16 cm, so 1.5 × IQR = 24 cm. A point is an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile: 166 + 24 = 190 cm. The maximum of 192 cm is therefore an outlier and would be plotted separately.
A student who measures 1.5 × IQR from the median rather than from the third quartile gets 158 + 24 = 182 cm. The rule uses the quartiles: the upper limit is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
A student who adds 1.5 × IQR to the first quartile instead of the third gets 150 + 24 = 174 cm. The upper limit is measured from the third quartile, and the lower limit from the first.

A student who takes the range (192 − 130 = 62 cm) as the interquartile range gets 1.5 × 62 = 93 and 166 + 93 = 259 cm. The IQR is the length of the box, Q3 − Q1 = 16 cm, not the full range of the data.
questions.explain: The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1 = 166 − 150 = 16 cm, so 1.5 × IQR = 24 cm. A point is an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile: 166 + 24 = 190 cm. The maximum of 192 cm is therefore an outlier and would be plotted separately.

questions.q: Two pea plants heterozygous for two unlinked genes (RrYy) are crossed. Why is the expected phenotypic ratio among their offspring 9:3:3:1?
options: The 16 cells of the Punnett grid contain four genotypes in the proportions 9:3:3:1, and each of these genotypes gives a different phenotype
Each parent makes four types of gamete and these combine with the single gamete type of the other parent in equal numbers, giving 9:3:3:1
Each gene independently gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive, and multiplying the probabilities gives 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 for the four phenotype combinations
Alleles inherited together stay together, so each parent makes only RY and ry gametes and these combine to give the four phenotype classes
optionWhy: A student who reads 9:3:3:1 as a genotypic ratio picks this. The grid contains nine different genotypes; 9:3:3:1 appears only when they are grouped by phenotype, the 9 class alone containing four genotypes.

A student who has confused the two dihybrid crosses picks this. Four gamete types meeting a single gamete type describes the test cross with a double homozygous recessive, which gives 1:1:1:1; here both parents make four gamete types.

Because the genes assort independently, the chance of round is 3/4 and of yellow 3/4, so round yellow is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16; round green and wrinkled yellow are each 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16; wrinkled green is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. The same result comes from a 16-cell Punnett grid of the four gamete types from each parent.

A student who thinks maternal and paternal alleles travel as sets picks this. Two gamete types from each parent would give only two phenotypes (round yellow and wrinkled green) in a 3:1 pattern, from three genotypes; independent assortment produces four gamete types, which is what generates the four phenotype classes in the 9:3:3:1 ratio.
questions.explain: Because the genes assort independently, the chance of round is 3/4 and of yellow 3/4, so round yellow is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16; round green and wrinkled yellow are each 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16; wrinkled green is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. The same result comes from a 16-cell Punnett grid of the four gamete types from each parent.

questions.q: A fly heterozygous for two linked genes (AaBb), which inherited the alleles A and B on one chromosome and a and b on the other, is test-crossed with an aabb fly. The offspring are 42 AaBb, 38 aabb, 11 Aabb and 9 aaBb. Which offspring are the recombinants, and what produced them?
options: The 42 AaBb and 38 aabb, because these offspring differ in genotype from the homozygous recessive parent
None of them, because two genes that are linked cannot give rise to any new combinations of their alleles
The 11 Aabb and 9 aaBb, produced by crossing over between the two loci in the heterozygous parent
All four classes, since a test cross of a double heterozygote gives four recombinant types in a 1:1:1:1 ratio
optionWhy: A student who reads 'recombinant' as 'different from a parent' picks this. Recombinants have new combinations of the heterozygote's alleles; AaBb received the parental AB chromosome and aabb the parental ab chromosome, so both are parental classes.

A student who thinks linkage is absolute picks this. Crossing over between the loci in some meioses produces Ab and aB gametes, and these recombinants are visible here as the 11 Aabb and 9 aaBb offspring.

The aabb parent contributes only ab gametes, so each offspring genotype reveals the gamete from the heterozygote. AB and ab gametes give the parental classes (42 and 38); Ab and aB gametes, formed only when crossing over occurs between the loci, give the two smaller recombinant classes (11 and 9, a recombination frequency of 20%).

A student who applies the unlinked test-cross ratio to every dihybrid picks this. The 1:1:1:1 ratio requires independent assortment; here the two classes of 42 and 38 far exceed the classes of 11 and 9, which is the pattern of linked genes with a minority of recombinants.
questions.explain: The aabb parent contributes only ab gametes, so each offspring genotype reveals the gamete from the heterozygote. AB and ab gametes give the parental classes (42 and 38); Ab and aB gametes, formed only when crossing over occurs between the loci, give the two smaller recombinant classes (11 and 9, a recombination frequency of 20%).

questions.q: Which statement about homeostasis in humans is correct?
options: Blood glucose concentration fluctuates within narrow preset limits around a set point.
Core body temperature is held at exactly 37 °C with no variation at all.
Skin temperature is kept within preset limits whatever the air temperature.
Blood pH is corrected only when it rises above its set point of about 7.4.
optionWhy: Homeostasis maintains the internal environment by keeping variables such as blood glucose concentration within preset limits. The value is not fixed: it rises after a meal and falls during fasting, and negative feedback keeps these swings within a narrow range around the set point.

A student who thinks homeostasis means perfect constancy picks this. Core temperature normally varies by a few tenths of a degree through the day; homeostasis keeps it within preset limits, not at one exact value.

A student who confuses the body's surface with its internal environment picks this. Skin temperature is allowed to vary widely; it is core temperature, blood pH, blood glucose and blood osmotic concentration that are the regulated variables.
A student who thinks homeostatic control acts in one direction only picks this. Blood pH is returned to the set point from values above and from values below it.
questions.explain: Homeostasis maintains the internal environment by keeping variables such as blood glucose concentration within preset limits. The value is not fixed: it rises after a meal and falls during fasting, and negative feedback keeps these swings within a narrow range around the set point.

questions.q: What is the physiological change that underlies type 2 diabetes?
options: Beta cells are destroyed by the immune system.
Beta cells are damaged by dietary sugar.
Insulin in the blood stops digesting glucose.
Target cells respond less to insulin.
optionWhy: A student who files both types of diabetes under 'no insulin' picks this. Autoimmune destruction of beta cells is the basis of type 1; in type 2 the cells are present and insulin is secreted, but its targets respond poorly.

A student who thinks sugar itself injures the pancreas picks this. A sugar-rich diet is a risk factor for type 2 because it contributes to obesity and insulin resistance, not because it destroys beta cells.
A student who treats insulin as an enzyme picks this. Insulin never digests glucose; it signals to cells to take glucose up. In type 2 diabetes the signal is sent but the cells respond weakly.

In type 2 diabetes insulin is secreted, at least in the early years, but liver, muscle and adipose cells have become insensitive to it, so glucose uptake falls and blood glucose stays high. This insulin resistance is why diet and exercise, which restore sensitivity, are the first treatments.
questions.explain: In type 2 diabetes insulin is secreted, at least in the early years, but liver, muscle and adipose cells have become insensitive to it, so glucose uptake falls and blood glucose stays high. This insulin resistance is why diet and exercise, which restore sensitivity, are the first treatments.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes osmoregulation from excretion?
options: Osmoregulation removes surplus water; excretion removes surplus solutes of every other kind.
Osmoregulation is carried out by the kidneys; excretion includes egestion of faeces by the gut.
Osmoregulation regulates the concentration of urea; excretion removes water from the body in urine.
Osmoregulation controls blood osmotic concentration; excretion removes metabolic waste.
optionWhy: A student who hears 'regulation' as 'removal' picks this. Osmoregulation may conserve water as well as discard it, and excretion concerns metabolic waste products specifically, not every solute.
A student who counts all waste leaving the body as excretion picks this. Faeces are mainly undigested food that never entered metabolism; their removal is egestion, not excretion.
A student who has swapped the two roles picks this. Urea removal is excretion; the regulated variable in osmoregulation is the osmotic concentration of the blood, not urea.

Osmoregulation is the regulation of the osmotic concentration of the blood (about 0.3 osmol L−1), achieved by adjusting water reabsorption. Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism, such as urea. The kidney does both, but they are separate roles.
questions.explain: Osmoregulation is the regulation of the osmotic concentration of the blood (about 0.3 osmol L−1), achieved by adjusting water reabsorption. Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism, such as urea. The kidney does both, but they are separate roles.

questions.q: How does the loop of Henle make it possible for the kidney to produce concentrated urine?
options: Its ascending limb actively transports water out of the filtrate and into the tiny blood vessels of the medulla.
It absorbs sodium ions into the filtrate so that the urine leaving the loop is already highly concentrated.
Its cells actively pump water into the collecting ducts, from which the blood then reabsorbs it directly.
Its ascending limb pumps sodium ions into the medulla, so water leaves the collecting ducts by osmosis.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the loop removes water directly picks this. Water is never actively transported, and the ascending limb is impermeable to water; it pumps sodium ions, and the water leaves later from the collecting ducts.

A student who has the direction of transport reversed picks this. Sodium ions are pumped out of the ascending limb into the medulla, so the fluid leaving the loop is actually dilute; the concentrating step happens in the collecting ducts.

A student who reaches for active transport to move water picks this. Water crosses the collecting duct wall by osmosis through aquaporins, driven by the high osmotic concentration the loop maintains in the medulla.

Active transport of sodium ions out of the ascending limb keeps the interstitial fluid of the medulla at a high osmotic concentration. The collecting ducts pass through this medulla, so when they are permeable to water it is drawn out of them by osmosis, concentrating the urine.
questions.explain: Active transport of sodium ions out of the ascending limb keeps the interstitial fluid of the medulla at a high osmotic concentration. The collecting ducts pass through this medulla, so when they are permeable to water it is drawn out of them by osmosis, concentrating the urine.
